questions.questionText: In an experiment testing how light affects plant growth, which variable is kept constant (controlled)?

options.label: A
options.text: Amount of water given to each plant

questions.explanation: Controlled variable = factor kept the same (water amount). Independent = light.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Null states no effect; alternative states there is an effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Null states there is an effect; alternative states no effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Both state there is an effect.

questions.explanation: Null = no effect/difference. Alternative = there IS an effect/difference.

questions.questionText: When is a bar chart most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Bar chart = comparing distinct categories.

questions.questionText: If a graph shows temperature rising steadily over time, this indicates:
questions.explanation: Rising steadily = positive correlation (both variables increase together).

questions.questionText: In an experiment on how fertilizer affects plant growth, what is the dependent variable?
questions.explanation: Dependent variable = what is measured (plant height). Independent = fertilizer.

questions.questionText: A conclusion is most valid when:

options.label: A
options.text: It is supported by repeated experimental data

questions.explanation: Validity comes from repeated experiments supporting the conclusion.

questions.questionText: A student measures the same length three times and gets slightly different values. This is due to:
questions.explanation: Random error = variation in repeated measurements.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of a control experiment?

options.label: A
options.text: To provide a baseline for comparison

questions.explanation: Control = baseline for comparison (no independent variable applied).

questions.questionText: Why do scientists repeat experiments?
questions.explanation: Repetition = check reliability and reduce random error.

questions.questionText: Express 4500 in scientific notation.
questions.explanation: 4500 = 4.5 × 10³ (move decimal 3 places left).

questions.questionText: What is the basic structure of the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Cell membrane = phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins (fluid mosaic model).

questions.questionText: Oxygen moves from the lungs into the blood by which process?
questions.explanation: Diffusion = movement of particles from high to low concentration (no energy needed).

questions.questionText: What happens to a plant cell in pure water?
questions.explanation: Water enters by osmosis → cell becomes turgid (turgor pressure).

questions.questionText: Active transport requires which molecule for energy?
questions.explanation: Active transport = movement against gradient using ATP (energy).

questions.questionText: According to the lock and key model, an enzyme:

options.label: A
options.text: Has a specific shape that fits its substrate

questions.explanation: Lock and key = enzyme has specific active site for substrate.
questions.subtopic: Enzyme function lock and key model

questions.questionText: What happens to enzyme activity at very high temperatures?
questions.explanation: High temperatures denature enzymes (active site shape changes).

questions.questionText: Most human enzymes work best at which pH?
questions.explanation: Most human enzymes work at pH 7 (neutral, body pH).

questions.questionText: Photosynthesis requires which input from sunlight?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert CO2 + H2O into glucose.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration?

options.label: A
options.text: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not

questions.explanation: Aerobic needs O2; anaerobic does not.

questions.questionText: What is the function of mitochondria in a cell?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria = powerhouse of cell (ATP production via respiration).

questions.questionText: How many food groups are in a balanced diet?
questions.explanation: Balanced diet = 7 food groups (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of carbohydrates in the body?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates = main energy source for body cells.

questions.questionText: What is the main function of proteins?
questions.explanation: Proteins = build and repair body tissues (muscles, skin, etc.).

questions.questionText: Which disease is caused by vitamin C deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency = scurvy (bleeding gums, weakness).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of vitamin D?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D = helps absorb calcium for strong bones.

questions.questionText: What is the function of iron in the body?

options.label: A
options.text: Part of hemoglobin in red blood cells

questions.explanation: Iron = essential for hemoglobin (carries oxygen in blood).

questions.questionText: What is the function of dietary fibre?
questions.explanation: Fibre = aids digestion, prevents constipation (roughage).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of water in the body?
questions.explanation: Water = hydration + solvent for body processes + temperature regulation.

questions.questionText: What is one effect of malnutrition?

options.label: A
options.text: Weak immune system and slow growth

questions.explanation: Malnutrition = weakness, slow growth, weak immunity.

questions.questionText: How is the energy content of food measured?
questions.explanation: Food energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ).

questions.questionText: Why is a water molecule polar?

options.label: A
options.text: Oxygen attracts electrons more strongly than hydrogen

questions.explanation: Oxygen is more electronegative → water has partial charges (δ+ on H, δ- on O).

questions.questionText: What is a hydrogen bond?

options.label: B
options.text: Chemical bond within one water molecule

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bond = attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ- O of another.

questions.questionText: In salt water, what is the solute?
questions.explanation: Solute = substance dissolved (salt). Solvent = substance doing dissolving (water).

questions.questionText: How does increasing temperature generally affect solubility of solids in water?
questions.explanation: For solids in water, solubility usually increases with temperature.

questions.questionText: A saturated solution is one that:

options.label: A
options.text: Cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature

questions.explanation: Saturated = maximum solute dissolved at that temperature.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between a solution and a suspension?

options.label: A
options.text: Solution is clear; suspension has visible particles

options.label: B
options.text: Solution has particles; suspension is clear

options.label: D
options.text: Solution is solid; suspension is liquid

questions.explanation: Solution = homogeneous (clear). Suspension = heterogeneous (visible particles).

questions.questionText: Why is water called the universal solvent?

options.label: A
options.text: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid

options.label: B
options.text: It is the most common liquid on Earth

questions.explanation: Water dissolves more substances than other liquids (due to polarity).

questions.questionText: During dissolving, what happens to solute particles?

options.label: A
options.text: They separate and spread throughout the solvent

options.label: C
options.text: They stay together as a clump

questions.explanation: Dissolving = solute particles separate and spread evenly in solvent.

questions.questionText: Which solution has more solute per unit volume?
questions.explanation: Concentrated = more solute per volume. Dilute = less solute per volume.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of filtration in water treatment?
questions.explanation: Filtration = removing solid particles by passing through filter.

questions.questionText: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
questions.explanation: pH 7 = neutral. Below 7 = acidic. Above 7 = alkaline.

questions.questionText: What colour does litmus turn in acid?
questions.explanation: Litmus turns red in acid, blue in alkali.

questions.questionText: What is the pH range of universal indicator?
questions.explanation: Universal indicator covers full pH range (1-14) with multiple colours.

questions.questionText: An acid is defined as a substance that:
questions.explanation: Acid (Brønsted-Lowry) = proton (H+) donor.

questions.questionText: An alkali is a substance that:
questions.explanation: Alkali = soluble base that releases OH- ions in water.

questions.questionText: What is produced when an acid reacts with an alkali?
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali = salt + water (neutralisation).

questions.questionText: What is one environmental effect of acid rain?
questions.explanation: Acid rain damages trees, lowers lake pH (harms aquatic life), erodes buildings.

questions.questionText: How do antacid tablets work in the stomach?
questions.explanation: Antacid = weak base that neutralises excess HCl in stomach.

questions.questionText: Which safety precaution is essential when handling corrosive acids?

options.label: D
options.text: Pour acid into eyes to test

questions.explanation: Safety: goggles + gloves + fume cupboard (never touch/smell directly).

questions.questionText: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?

options.label: A
options.text: Strong acid ionises completely; weak acid ionises partially

options.label: B
options.text: Strong acid is solid; weak acid is liquid

options.label: C
options.text: Strong acid is hot; weak acid is cold

questions.explanation: Strong acid = fully ionised in water. Weak acid = partially ionised.

questions.questionText: A car travels 100 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance / time = 100 km / 2 h = 50 km/h.

questions.questionText: Why is velocity called a vector quantity?

options.label: A
options.text: It has both magnitude and direction

questions.explanation: Vector = magnitude + direction. Velocity is speed in a specific direction.

questions.questionText: What is the formula for acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity / time = (v - u) / t.

questions.questionText: What does Newton's first law state?

options.label: A
options.text: An object at rest stays at rest; an object in motion stays in motion (unless force acts).

options.label: C
options.text: Every action has equal opposite reaction

questions.explanation: Newton 1st law = inertia (object maintains state of motion unless force acts).
questions.subtopic: Newton first law inertia state of motion

questions.questionText: What is Newton's second law?

options.label: A
options.text: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = m × a)

options.label: B
options.text: Every action has equal opposite reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Objects at rest stay at rest

options.label: D
options.text: Energy cannot be created or destroyed

questions.explanation: Newton 2nd law: F = m × a (force = mass × acceleration).
questions.subtopic: Newton second law F equals ma

questions.questionText: What does Newton's third law state?

options.label: A
options.text: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction

options.label: C
options.text: Objects at rest stay at rest

questions.explanation: Newton 3rd law = action-reaction pairs (equal magnitude, opposite direction).
questions.subtopic: Newton third law equal opposite forces

questions.questionText: What is the difference between mass and weight?

options.label: A
options.text: Mass = amount of matter; weight = force of gravity on mass

options.label: C
options.text: Mass changes with location; weight doesn't

questions.explanation: Mass (kg) = matter. Weight (N) = gravitational force on mass.

questions.questionText: What is the direction of friction on a moving object?

options.label: A
options.text: Opposite to the direction of motion

options.label: B
options.text: Same as the direction of motion

questions.explanation: Friction always opposes motion (kinetic friction acts against movement).

questions.questionText: What is the approximate acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² ≈ 10 m/s² (free fall acceleration).

questions.questionText: What is the formula for momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity (p = m × v).

questions.questionText: In a uniform medium, how does light travel?
questions.explanation: Rectilinear propagation = light travels in straight lines in uniform medium.

questions.questionText: A light ray hits a mirror at 30° to the normal. According to the law of reflection, what is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 30°.

questions.questionText: What is refraction?

options.label: A
options.text: Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another

options.label: B
options.text: Reflection of light from a surface

questions.explanation: Refraction = light bending when passing between media of different densities.

questions.questionText: What is the property of a convex lens?

options.label: A
options.text: Converges light rays to a focal point

questions.explanation: Convex (converging) lens = focuses parallel rays to a focal point.

questions.questionText: What is the property of a concave lens?
questions.explanation: Concave (diverging) lens = spreads light rays apart.

questions.questionText: In an optical fibre, total internal reflection allows light to travel because:

options.label: A
options.text: Light reflects inside the glass core due to angle of incidence exceeding critical angle

options.label: D
options.text: Light travels in straight lines only

questions.explanation: TIR: light enters fibre at angle > critical angle, reflects internally along fibre.

questions.questionText: What is the image formed by a plane mirror?

options.label: A
options.text: Same size, upright, virtual, laterally inverted

questions.explanation: Plane mirror = same size, upright, virtual, laterally inverted (reversed left-right).

questions.questionText: What is the speed of light in vacuum?
questions.explanation: Speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (≈300,000 km/s).

questions.questionText: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red has the longest wavelength (~700 nm); violet has the shortest (~400 nm).

questions.questionText: Long-sightedness (hyperopia) is corrected using which lens?
questions.explanation: Long-sightedness = converging (convex) lens focuses near objects on retina.

questions.questionText: Convert 27°C to Kelvin.
What does specific heat capacity measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity = energy (J) to raise 1 kg of substance by 1°C.

questions.questionText: Why are metals good conductors of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals have free electrons that transfer heat energy through collision.

questions.questionText: In which state of matter does convection occur?
questions.explanation: Convection = heat transfer by fluid movement (liquids and gases).

questions.questionText: Why can radiation transfer heat through a vacuum?

options.label: A
options.text: Radiation uses electromagnetic waves (no medium needed)

questions.explanation: Radiation = electromagnetic waves (can travel through vacuum, e.g., Sun's heat).

questions.questionText: What is latent heat of fusion?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy needed to melt 1 kg of solid at its melting point

questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion = energy to melt 1 kg solid (no temperature change).

questions.questionText: What does Brownian motion demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Brownian motion (pollen in water) = evidence of moving particles in matter.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between heat and temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: Heat is energy; temperature measures average kinetic energy

questions.explanation: Heat = energy transfer. Temperature = average kinetic energy of particles.

questions.questionText: During the day, what causes a sea breeze?

options.label: A
options.text: Land heats faster than sea; air rises over land; cool sea air moves in

questions.explanation: Sea breeze = land heats faster → hot air rises over land → cool air from sea replaces it.

questions.questionText: Which of these is the best thermal insulator?
questions.explanation: Wood is a thermal insulator (low thermal conductivity).

questions.questionText: In a metal wire, electric current is the flow of:
questions.explanation: Current in metals = flow of free electrons.

questions.questionText: What is voltage (potential difference)?
questions.explanation: Voltage (V) = energy transferred per unit charge (J/C).

questions.questionText: What is Ohm's law?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law: V = I × R (voltage = current × resistance).
questions.subtopic: Resistance ohms law V equals IR

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, what is the same throughout?
questions.explanation: Series circuit = same current through all components.

questions.questionText: In a parallel circuit, what is the same across each branch?
questions.explanation: Parallel circuit = same voltage across each branch.

questions.questionText: What is the function of a fuse?

options.label: A
options.text: To break circuit when current is too high

questions.explanation: Fuse = safety device that melts and breaks circuit if current exceeds limit.

questions.questionText: What is the function of the earth wire?

options.label: A
options.text: To carry current safely to ground if fault occurs

questions.explanation: Earth wire = safety wire that carries leakage current to ground (prevents shock).

questions.questionText: What is the colour of the live wire in Malaysian mains wiring?
questions.explanation: Live wire = brown. Neutral = blue. Earth = green-yellow stripes.

questions.questionText: What is the frequency of Malaysian mains electricity?
questions.explanation: Malaysian mains frequency = 50 Hz (alternating current).

questions.questionText: A kettle has a power rating of 2 kW. How many watts is this?
What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
questions.explanation: DNA = double helix (two strands twisted around each other).

questions.questionText: What is a gene?

options.label: A
options.text: A section of DNA that codes for a trait

questions.explanation: Gene = section of DNA coding for a specific characteristic.

questions.questionText: In genetics, what is a dominant allele?

options.label: A
options.text: An allele that masks the effect of another

questions.explanation: Dominant allele = expressed even when paired with recessive allele.

questions.questionText: What is a Punnett square used for?
questions.explanation: Punnett square = diagram showing possible offspring genotypes from parents.

questions.questionText: How many chromosomes are in a typical human body cell?
questions.explanation: Human body cell = 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of mitosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Growth and repair of body cells

questions.explanation: Mitosis = cell division for growth and tissue repair (produces 2 identical cells).

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis = cell division producing gametes (sperm/egg) with half chromosomes.

questions.questionText: What is formed when a sperm cell fertilises an egg cell?
questions.explanation: Fertilisation: sperm + egg = zygote (fertilised egg).

questions.questionText: Eye colour is an example of which type of variation?
questions.explanation: Eye colour = inherited (from parents via genes).

questions.questionText: What is genetic modification (GM)?

options.label: A
options.text: Changing an organism's DNA to give it new traits

questions.explanation: GM = inserting/modifying genes to give organism new characteristics.

questions.questionText: A scientist predicts that 'If plants receive more sunlight, they will grow taller.' Which part is the hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Plants receiving more sunlight will grow taller

questions.explanation: Hypothesis = testable prediction (If X, then Y).

questions.questionText: When designing a data table for measuring length, what must be included in the column heading?
questions.explanation: Heading should include quantity + unit (length/cm).
questions.subtopic: Data table design with units basic

questions.questionText: What must be labelled on the x-axis and y-axis of a bar graph?

options.label: A
options.text: Variable name and unit on both axes

questions.explanation: Both axes need variable + unit for clear interpretation.

questions.questionText: When a line graph shows data points scattered but with a clear trend, what should be drawn?

options.label: A
options.text: A best-fit line through the data

questions.explanation: Best-fit line shows the overall trend through scattered data.

questions.questionText: If a pie chart shows that 25% of students like Maths, what fraction of the circle does this represent?
questions.explanation: 25% = 1/4 of the pie chart (90° angle).

questions.questionText: A study concludes 'Exercise improves health' but only tested 5 people. What is the main limitation?
questions.explanation: Limitation = small sample cannot represent whole population.

questions.questionText: In a fair test to compare effectiveness of two fertilizers, what must be kept the same?

options.label: A
options.text: All variables except the fertilizer type

questions.explanation: Fair test = change only the independent variable (fertilizer type).

questions.questionText: If three trials give measurements of 8 cm, 10 cm, and 9 cm, what is the mean?
If measurements are very close to the true value but vary slightly between trials, this shows:
questions.explanation: Accuracy = close to true value. Precision = reproducibility.

questions.questionText: Which is an example of quantitative data?
questions.explanation: Quantitative = numerical (25°C). Qualitative = descriptive.

questions.questionText: Which structure contains the genetic material (DNA) in an animal cell?
questions.explanation: Nucleus contains DNA (genetic material) and controls cell activities.

questions.questionText: Which structure is found ONLY in plant cells (not animal cells)?
questions.explanation: Cell wall = unique to plant cells (cellulose).

questions.questionText: Which is a difference between animal and plant cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Plant cells have cell wall; animal cells do not

options.label: B
options.text: Animal cells have nucleus; plant cells do not

options.label: C
options.text: Animal cells have cytoplasm; plant cells do not

questions.explanation: Plant cells have cell wall + chloroplasts + large vacuole (animal cells don't).
questions.subtopic: Animal vs plant cell difference distinction

questions.questionText: What is the function of the nucleus in a cell?
questions.explanation: Nucleus = control centre (DNA directs cell activities).

questions.questionText: What happens in the cytoplasm of a cell?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm = jelly-like substance where many reactions occur.

questions.questionText: In which organelle does photosynthesis occur?
questions.explanation: Chloroplast = site of photosynthesis (contains chlorophyll).

questions.questionText: What is the function of ribosomes in a cell?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes = protein synthesis site.

questions.questionText: What is the main function of the cell wall in plant cells?
questions.explanation: Cell wall = rigid support (cellulose) in plant cells.

questions.questionText: What is the main function of the vacuole in plant cells?
questions.explanation: Vacuole = storage of water, sugars, waste (large in plant cells).

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between diffusion and osmosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Diffusion is movement of any particles; osmosis is water across membrane

options.label: C
options.text: Osmosis needs energy; diffusion does not

questions.explanation: Diffusion = any particles. Osmosis = water only across semi-permeable membrane.

questions.questionText: What colour does iodine solution turn when starch is present?
questions.explanation: Iodine + starch = blue-black colour.

questions.questionText: What colour change indicates a positive Benedict's test for sugar (when heated)?
questions.explanation: Benedict's + reducing sugar (heated) = blue → orange/brick red.

questions.questionText: What colour indicates a positive Biuret test for protein?
questions.explanation: Biuret + protein = blue → purple/violet colour.

questions.questionText: How is fat tested using ethanol?

options.label: A
options.text: Ethanol dissolves fat; paper becomes translucent when dry

questions.explanation: Ethanol dissolves fat, leaving translucent stain on paper.

questions.questionText: What is the main function of vitamin A?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A = healthy eyesight and skin.

questions.questionText: What is the main function of vitamin B complex?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B = energy release from food (metabolism).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of vitamin C?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain healthy skin, gums, and immunity

questions.explanation: Vitamin C = healthy gums, skin, immunity (antioxidant).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of vitamin K?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K = blood clotting (wound healing).
questions.subtopic: Vitamin K function blood clotting basic

questions.questionText: What is the main function of calcium?
questions.explanation: Calcium = strong bones and teeth (with vitamin D).

questions.questionText: What is the function of the mineral iodine in the body?
questions.explanation: Iodine = needed by thyroid gland for metabolism regulation.

questions.questionText: What is the solvent in a salt solution?
questions.explanation: Solvent = substance that does the dissolving (water in salt water).

questions.questionText: What is the solute in a sugar solution?
questions.explanation: Solute = substance being dissolved (sugar in sugar water).

questions.questionText: How does increasing temperature affect the solubility of gases in water?
questions.explanation: Gas solubility DECREASES with increasing temperature (opposite of solids).

questions.questionText: How is crystallisation used to separate a solid from a solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporate water to leave solid crystals

options.label: C
options.text: Heat the solution and condense vapour

questions.explanation: Crystallisation = evaporating solvent to form solid crystals.

questions.questionText: What does filtration separate?
questions.explanation: Filtration = separates insoluble solid from liquid (using filter paper).

questions.questionText: What does evaporation separate?
questions.explanation: Evaporation = separates dissolved solute from solvent (by heating).

questions.questionText: What is distillation used to produce?
questions.explanation: Distillation = boiling + condensing to get pure solvent.

questions.questionText: What does paper chromatography separate?

options.label: A
options.text: Different coloured substances in a mixture

questions.explanation: Chromatography = separates dissolved substances based on solubility.

questions.questionText: If 30 g of sugar dissolves in 100 g of water at 25°C, what is the solubility?
questions.explanation: Solubility = mass of solute per 100 g solvent (30 g/100 g).

questions.questionText: What happens to a solution's concentration when more water is added?
questions.explanation: Adding solvent (water) decreases concentration.

questions.questionText: Which is an example of a strong acid?
questions.explanation: Strong acids: HCl, H2SO4, HNO3 (fully ionised in water).

questions.questionText: Which is an example of a weak acid?
questions.explanation: Weak acids: citric, ethanoic, carbonic (partially ionised).

questions.questionText: Which is an example of an alkali?
questions.explanation: Common alkalis: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)2 (soluble bases).

questions.questionText: What is a natural indicator?

options.label: A
options.text: A substance from plants that changes colour in acid/alkali

questions.explanation: Natural indicators: litmus (lichens), red cabbage, turmeric.

questions.questionText: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strong alkali?
questions.explanation: Universal indicator: strong alkali (pH 12-14) = purple/dark blue.

questions.questionText: What salt is formed when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O (sodium chloride + water).

questions.questionText: Why must you wear goggles when handling concentrated acids?
questions.explanation: Concentrated acids are corrosive — eye protection prevents serious injury.

questions.questionText: What should you do if alkali splashes on your skin?

options.label: A
options.text: Wash immediately with plenty of water

questions.explanation: Alkalis are corrosive — immediate water rinse is critical.

questions.questionText: Most plants grow best in soil with pH around:
questions.explanation: Most plants grow in slightly acidic to neutral soil (pH 6-7).
questions.subtopic: Soil pH acidic alkaline plant growth

questions.questionText: Why does milk of magnesia help with indigestion?
questions.explanation: Antacid = weak base that neutralises excess HCl in stomach.

questions.questionText: A person walks 5 m east then 5 m west. What is the distance travelled?
questions.explanation: Distance = total path (10 m). Displacement = net change (0 m).

questions.questionText: Speed is a scalar quantity because it has:
questions.explanation: Scalar = magnitude only. Vector = magnitude + direction.

questions.questionText: If a car slows down from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s, what is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (v - u)/t = (10 - 20)/5 = -2 m/s² (negative = deceleration).

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.explanation: Mass SI unit = kilogram (kg).

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force SI unit = newton (N). 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s².

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of weight?
questions.explanation: Weight = force, measured in newtons (N).

questions.questionText: If two forces of 5 N act on an object in opposite directions, what is the net force?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces (equal, opposite) = net force 0 N (no acceleration).

questions.questionText: What happens when unbalanced forces act on a stationary object?

options.label: A
options.text: It accelerates in the direction of the net force

questions.explanation: Unbalanced forces → net force ≠ 0 → acceleration occurs.

questions.questionText: What does inertia mean?
questions.explanation: Inertia = tendency of object to resist change in motion (Newton 1st law).

questions.questionText: How does doubling the speed of a car affect its stopping distance?
questions.explanation: Stopping distance ∝ speed² (4× speed = 4× distance).

questions.questionText: Which is an example of a natural light source?
questions.explanation: Natural light source = Sun, stars, fire (from nature). Artificial = human-made.

questions.questionText: What is the approximate speed of light in vacuum?
questions.explanation: Speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.questionText: What is diffuse reflection?
questions.explanation: Diffuse reflection = rough surface scatters light in many directions.

questions.questionText: What is specular reflection?
questions.explanation: Specular reflection = smooth surface reflects parallel rays.

questions.questionText: Why does light refract when it enters a different medium?

options.label: A
options.text: Light travels at different speeds in different media

questions.explanation: Refraction = bending due to change in speed when entering different medium.

questions.questionText: What is the focal point of a lens?

options.label: A
options.text: Point where parallel light rays converge after passing through lens

questions.explanation: Focal point = where parallel rays converge (convex) or appear to diverge (concave).

questions.questionText: What is a real image?

options.label: A
options.text: Image formed by actual light rays meeting at a point

questions.explanation: Real image = formed by actual rays (can be projected on screen).

questions.questionText: What is a virtual image?

options.label: A
options.text: Image formed where light appears to come from (cannot be projected)

questions.explanation: Virtual image = rays appear to come from a point (cannot be projected).

questions.questionText: What type of lens is used in a magnifying glass?
questions.explanation: Magnifying glass = convex lens (converges light to magnify image).

questions.questionText: In a simple camera, what kind of image is formed on the film/sensor?
questions.explanation: Camera forms real, inverted, smaller image on film/sensor.
questions.subtopic: Camera simple convex lens image formation

questions.questionText: How does a typical liquid thermometer work?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid expands when heated and rises in tube

questions.explanation: Thermometer = liquid (mercury/alcohol) expands with heat, rises in tube.

questions.questionText: A cup of water at 80°C has more thermal energy than the same cup at 20°C. What does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher temperature means more thermal energy (heat) at same mass

questions.explanation: Higher temperature = more average KE = more thermal energy (heat) for same mass.

questions.questionText: Calculate heat needed: m = 2 kg, c = 400 J/(kg·°C), ΔT = 5°C.
questions.subtopic: Specific heat capacity calculation Q equals mc delta T

questions.questionText: What is latent heat of vaporisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy to change 1 kg liquid to gas (no temperature change)

questions.explanation: Latent heat of vaporisation = energy to boil 1 kg liquid.

questions.questionText: How does a radiator heat a room by convection?

options.label: A
options.text: Hot air rises; cool air sinks; creates circulation

questions.explanation: Radiator heats air → hot air rises → cool air replaces → convection current.

questions.questionText: Which material is the best conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Metals (free electrons) conduct heat best; plastic/wood/rubber are insulators.

questions.questionText: Which surface emits thermal radiation best?
questions.explanation: Dull dark surfaces emit thermal radiation better than shiny surfaces.

questions.questionText: Which method of heat transfer can work in vacuum?
questions.explanation: Radiation = electromagnetic waves (works in vacuum). Conduction/convection need medium.

questions.questionText: During the day at the beach, what causes the sea breeze?

options.label: A
options.text: Land heats faster than sea; hot air over land rises; cool sea air moves in

questions.explanation: Sea breeze = land heats faster → hot air rises over land → cool sea air flows in.
questions.subtopic: Sea breeze land breeze day night

questions.questionText: Why are small gaps left between sections of railway track?

options.label: A
options.text: To allow for thermal expansion in hot weather

questions.explanation: Rails expand when heated; gaps prevent buckling.

questions.questionText: How is static electricity produced?

options.label: A
options.text: By friction between two materials (electrons transfer)

questions.explanation: Static electricity = charge imbalance from friction (electron transfer).

questions.questionText: What happens when two negatively charged objects are brought close together?
questions.explanation: Like charges repel (+/+, -/-). Opposite charges attract.

questions.questionText: What is an electric field?

options.label: A
options.text: Region where electric charges experience a force

questions.explanation: Electric field = region around charge where other charges feel force.

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: Current SI unit = ampere (A).

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of voltage?
questions.explanation: Voltage SI unit = volt (V).

questions.questionText: What is the SI unit of resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance SI unit = ohm (Ω).

questions.questionText: Calculate voltage: I = 2 A, R = 5 Ω.
questions.subtopic: Ohm law calculation V equals IR example

questions.questionText: Two resistors (3 Ω and 6 Ω) are in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.explanation: Series: R_total = R1 + R2 = 3 + 6 = 9 Ω.

questions.questionText: Three identical bulbs are connected in parallel to a 6V battery. What is the voltage across each bulb?
questions.explanation: Parallel = same voltage across each branch (= battery voltage = 6 V).

questions.questionText: Calculate power: V = 12 V, I = 3 A.
questions.subtopic: Power calculation P equals VI example

questions.questionText: What is heredity?

options.label: A
options.text: Passing of traits from parents to offspring

questions.explanation: Heredity = passing traits from parents to offspring via genes.

questions.questionText: What is a genotype?

options.label: A
options.text: The genetic makeup of an organism (letters)

questions.explanation: Genotype = genetic makeup (e.g., Bb, BB, bb).

questions.questionText: What is a phenotype?

options.label: A
options.text: The observable physical traits of an organism

questions.explanation: Phenotype = observable traits (e.g., tall, short, brown eyes).

questions.questionText: What does homozygous mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Two identical alleles for a trait (e.g., BB or bb)

questions.explanation: Homozygous = two identical alleles (BB or bb).

questions.questionText: What does heterozygous mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Two different alleles for a trait (e.g., Bb)

questions.explanation: Heterozygous = two different alleles (Bb).

questions.questionText: What sex chromosomes does a human male have?
questions.explanation: Male = XY (one X, one Y). Female = XX.

questions.questionText: Haemophilia is an example of what type of inheritance?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia = sex-linked recessive (X chromosome).

questions.questionText: What is a mutation?
questions.explanation: Mutation = random change in DNA sequence (can cause variation).

questions.questionText: What is selective breeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Choosing parents with desired traits to breed

questions.explanation: Selective breeding = humans choose parents with desired traits to produce offspring.

questions.questionText: What is cloning?

options.label: A
options.text: Producing genetically identical copies of an organism

questions.explanation: Cloning = making genetically identical copy (asexual reproduction in lab).

questions.questionText: A student notes that 'the solution turned blue'. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Observation = direct description using senses; no explanation needed.

questions.questionText: If a student concludes that 'the plant is wilting because it needs water' based on dry soil, this is:
questions.explanation: Inference = explanation/interpretation from observation.

questions.questionText: What makes a statement a scientific hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.text: It must be testable and falsifiable

questions.explanation: Hypothesis = testable statement that can be supported or refuted.

questions.questionText: In an experiment, the variable kept the same throughout is called:
questions.explanation: Controlled variable = kept constant (not changed).

questions.questionText: What is the most important first step when recording experimental data?

options.label: A
options.text: Note units and use a systematic table

questions.explanation: Record raw data with units in systematic tables.

questions.questionText: Which graph is most suitable for showing how a plant's height changes over several weeks?
questions.explanation: Line graph = continuous variable over time (e.g., height vs days).

questions.questionText: A scientific conclusion should always be:
questions.explanation: Conclusion = must be supported by evidence, not by belief.

questions.questionText: A study using only 3 participants has what type of limitation?
questions.explanation: Limitation = small sample cannot represent whole population.

questions.questionText: Why do scientific journals use peer review?

options.label: A
options.text: To validate quality and accuracy of research

questions.explanation: Peer review = experts check research quality before publication.

questions.questionText: Which is the correct order of the scientific method?
questions.explanation: Scientific method: observe → hypothesis → experiment → analyse → conclude.

questions.questionText: Which is NOT one of the three principles of cell theory?

options.label: A
options.text: All cells come from non-living matter

options.label: B
options.text: All living things are made of cells

options.label: C
options.text: All cells come from pre-existing cells

options.label: D
options.text: The cell is the basic unit of life

questions.explanation: Cell theory: (1) all organisms made of cells, (2) cell is basic unit, (3) all cells from pre-existing cells.

questions.questionText: In a plant cell, what is the main function of the chloroplast?
questions.explanation: Chloroplast = site of photosynthesis (chlorophyll absorbs light).

questions.questionText: Why does the large central vacuole in a mature plant cell provide support?

options.label: A
options.text: Water inside pushes against cell wall (turgor)

questions.explanation: Vacuole full of water pushes against cell wall = turgor pressure (support).
questions.subtopic: Plant cell large central vacuole function

questions.questionText: Where in the cell does aerobic respiration occur?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria = site of aerobic respiration (ATP production).

questions.questionText: Where in a cell are proteins synthesised?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes = protein synthesis (translation of mRNA).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)?

options.label: A
options.text: Transport of materials within the cell

questions.explanation: ER = network of tubes for transporting materials (especially proteins).

questions.questionText: What is the function of the Golgi apparatus?

options.label: A
options.text: Modify, sort, and package proteins for transport

questions.explanation: Golgi apparatus = modifies and packages proteins for secretion.

questions.questionText: What does it mean for the cell membrane to be selectively permeable?

options.label: A
options.text: Some substances pass through; others are blocked

questions.explanation: Selective permeability = some substances through, others blocked.

questions.questionText: What is the main structural component of a plant cell wall?
questions.explanation: Plant cell wall = cellulose (rigid structure).

questions.questionText: What is the function of plasmodesmata in plant cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Allow communication between adjacent plant cells

questions.explanation: Plasmodesmata = channels through cell walls connecting plant cells.

questions.questionText: If energy intake equals energy expenditure, the body's weight:
questions.explanation: Energy balance = intake = expenditure → stable weight.

questions.questionText: Which is a complex carbohydrate?
questions.explanation: Complex carbohydrates = starch (long chains). Simple = glucose, sucrose.

questions.questionText: What makes a protein 'complete'?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains all essential amino acids

questions.explanation: Complete protein = contains all essential amino acids (animal sources).
questions.subtopic: Protein complete incomplete essential amino acids

questions.questionText: Which type of fat is healthier for the heart?
questions.explanation: Unsaturated fats (vegetable oils, fish) = better for heart than saturated/trans fats.

questions.questionText: Which deficiency causes night blindness?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency = night blindness (poor vision in dim light).

questions.questionText: What disease is caused by Vitamin C deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency = scurvy (bleeding gums, weakness).
questions.subtopic: Vitamin C deficiency scurvy bleeding gums

questions.questionText: Which deficiency causes rickets in children?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency = rickets (soft, weak bones in children).
questions.subtopic: Vitamin D deficiency rickets bone weakness

questions.questionText: What is a symptom of iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency = anaemia (tiredness, pale skin).

questions.questionText: Iodine deficiency affects which gland?
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency = goitre (swollen thyroid in neck).

questions.questionText: What is the main function of dietary fibre?

options.label: A
options.text: Promote healthy digestion and prevent constipation

questions.explanation: Dietary fibre = adds bulk to food, prevents constipation (roughage).

questions.questionText: Water has a high specific heat capacity. This means it:

options.label: A
options.text: Heats up and cools down slowly

questions.explanation: High specific heat = water changes temperature slowly (good for cooling).
questions.subtopic: Water specific heat capacity high property

questions.questionText: What property of water molecules makes water an excellent solvent?

options.label: A
options.text: Water polarity allows it to dissolve many ionic and polar substances

options.label: C
options.text: Water has no charge at all

questions.explanation: Water polarity allows it to dissolve many ionic and polar substances.

questions.questionText: A solution contains 20 g of sugar in 100 mL water. What is its concentration?
questions.explanation: Concentration = mass of solute / volume of solvent (20 g / 100 mL).

questions.questionText: From a solubility curve, if solubility at 40°C is 50 g/100 g water, how much solute can dissolve?

options.label: A
options.text: 50 g of solute in 100 g of water

options.label: B
options.text: 40 g of solute in 100 g of water

options.label: C
options.text: 100 g of solute in 50 g of water

questions.explanation: Solubility curve = gives max g solute per 100 g solvent at given temperature.

questions.questionText: How can salt be obtained from sea water?
questions.explanation: Evaporation = heating to remove water leaves salt crystals.
questions.subtopic: Crystallisation salt from sea water method

questions.questionText: Which laboratory equipment is needed for filtration?
questions.explanation: Filtration requires filter paper + funnel + beaker to separate insoluble solid from liquid.

questions.questionText: Evaporation followed by crystallisation is used to:
questions.explanation: Evaporation + crystallisation = recover dissolved solid (solute).

questions.questionText: What is the principle of simple distillation?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporate and condense liquid to obtain pure solvent

questions.explanation: Distillation = evaporate then condense to purify liquid.

questions.questionText: Fractional distillation separates liquids based on differences in their:
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation separates liquids by different boiling points.

questions.questionText: Paper chromatography separates substances based on differences in their:
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates by different solubilities in solvent.

questions.questionText: On the pH scale, which value represents a strong acid?
questions.explanation: pH 1 = strong acid. pH 7 = neutral. pH 14 = strong alkali.
questions.subtopic: pH scale 0 to 14 measurement acidic alkaline

questions.questionText: Blue litmus turns what colour in acid?
questions.explanation: Blue litmus → red in acid. Red litmus → blue in alkali.
questions.subtopic: Litmus red blue colour change indicator

questions.questionText: Universal indicator shows the full range of pH from:
questions.explanation: Universal indicator covers pH 1 (red) to pH 14 (purple).

questions.questionText: When an acid reacts with a metal like magnesium, what gas is released?
questions.explanation: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas.

questions.questionText: When acid reacts with a carbonate, which gas is released?
questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂ gas.

questions.questionText: What are the products of a neutralisation reaction?
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation).

questions.questionText: What environmental problem is caused by emissions of SO₂ and NOₓ from vehicles?
questions.explanation: SO₂ + NOₓ emissions from vehicles form acidic gases that dissolve in rainwater = acid rain.
questions.subtopic: Acid rain sulphur dioxide nitrogen oxide

questions.questionText: Antacid tablets work by:
questions.explanation: Antacids = weak bases that neutralise excess HCl in stomach.

questions.questionText: Farmers add lime (calcium hydroxide) to acidic soil to:

options.label: A
options.text: Neutralise the acidity and improve crop growth

questions.explanation: Lime = base that neutralises acidic soil for plant growth.

questions.questionText: Which safety precaution is most essential when handling acids in a lab?

options.label: A
options.text: Wear goggles, gloves, and work in a fume cupboard

options.label: C
options.text: Pour acid onto your hand first

questions.explanation: Always use goggles + gloves + fume cupboard for acid work.
questions.subtopic: Acid safety lab goggles gloves basic

questions.questionText: Which quantity has BOTH size and direction?
questions.explanation: Vectors have both magnitude and direction (force, velocity, acceleration).

questions.questionText: A straight horizontal line on a distance-time graph shows:
questions.explanation: Horizontal line on distance-time graph = object stationary (at rest).
questions.subtopic: Distance time graph straight line constant speed

questions.questionText: On a velocity-time graph, what does the slope of the line represent?
questions.explanation: Slope of velocity-time graph = acceleration (change in velocity).
questions.subtopic: Velocity time graph horizontal line constant

questions.questionText: What does negative acceleration mean?
questions.explanation: Negative acceleration = deceleration (slowing down) if velocity is positive.

questions.questionText: Why is force drawn as an arrow (vector) in physics diagrams?

options.label: A
options.text: To show magnitude and direction of the force

questions.explanation: Arrow length = magnitude, direction = direction of force.

questions.questionText: Which of these is measured in kilograms?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in kg. Weight is measured in newtons (N).

questions.questionText: Inertia of an object depends on its:
questions.explanation: Inertia ∝ mass (more mass = more inertia).

questions.questionText: Which state of motion does Newton's first law describe?
questions.explanation: Newton 1st law = object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless force acts.
questions.subtopic: Newton first law rest motion continuation

questions.questionText: According to Newton's second law, force is proportional to:
questions.explanation: Newton 2nd law: F = m × a (force ∝ mass × acceleration).
questions.subtopic: Newton second law force proportional acceleration

questions.questionText: When you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Newton 3rd law = every action has equal and opposite reaction.
questions.subtopic: Newton third law action reaction pair

questions.questionText: Light is part of which type of wave?
questions.explanation: Light = electromagnetic wave (no medium needed to travel).

questions.questionText: If a light ray hits a mirror at 45° to the normal, what is the angle of reflection?
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection = 45°.
questions.subtopic: Reflection law angle incidence angle reflection

questions.questionText: What type of image is formed by a plane mirror?

options.label: A
options.text: Virtual, upright, same size as object

questions.explanation: Plane mirror = virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted.
questions.subtopic: Plane mirror image virtual upright same size

questions.questionText: A concave mirror is also called:
questions.explanation: Concave mirror = converging (parallel rays converge at focal point).

questions.questionText: Where are convex mirrors commonly used?

options.label: A
options.text: Vehicle side mirrors (wider field of view)

questions.explanation: Convex mirror = diverging (wider view), used in side mirrors/shop security.

questions.questionText: What happens to the speed of light when it enters glass from air?
questions.explanation: Light slows down when entering denser medium (glass).

questions.questionText: Snell's law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to:

options.label: A
options.text: The refractive index of the medium

questions.explanation: Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ (refractive index).

questions.questionText: An object placed beyond the focal length of a convex lens forms:
questions.explanation: Convex lens with object beyond focal length → real, inverted image.
questions.subtopic: Convex lens converging image real inverted

questions.questionText: An object placed anywhere in front of a concave lens forms:
questions.explanation: Concave (diverging) lens always produces virtual, upright, smaller image.
questions.subtopic: Concave lens diverging image virtual upright

questions.questionText: Total internal reflection happens when light travels from:

options.label: A
options.text: Denser to less dense medium at critical angle

questions.explanation: TIR: light goes from denser to less dense, beyond critical angle.

questions.questionText: Temperature is a measure of the:

options.label: B
options.text: Total heat energy of a substance

questions.explanation: Temperature = average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.

questions.questionText: What is heat?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy transferred between objects of different temperatures

questions.explanation: Heat = energy transfer due to temperature difference.

questions.questionText: Why is water useful as a coolant in car engines?

options.label: A
options.text: Water absorbs much heat with little temperature rise

questions.explanation: Water has high specific heat capacity = absorbs much heat with small temp rise.

questions.questionText: How does heat transfer by conduction occur in a metal?

options.label: A
options.text: Vibrating particles pass energy to neighbouring particles

questions.explanation: Conduction = vibrating particles transfer kinetic energy to neighbours.

questions.questionText: Convection occurs only in:
questions.explanation: Convection requires fluid movement (liquids + gases).

questions.questionText: Why can the Sun heat the Earth through the vacuum of space?

options.label: A
options.text: Infrared radiation (EM waves) can travel through vacuum

options.label: B
options.text: Hot air carries heat across space

questions.explanation: Sun's heat travels as infrared radiation (EM waves) through space vacuum to Earth.

questions.questionText: Which is the best conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Copper (metal) is excellent heat conductor (free electrons).

questions.questionText: Which is the best heat insulator?
questions.explanation: Fibreglass = good insulator (traps air). Metals are conductors.

questions.questionText: The principle of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is:

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid expands when heated, contracts when cooled

questions.explanation: Mercury/alcohol expands/contracts uniformly with temperature.

questions.questionText: What is specific latent heat of melting?

options.label: A
options.text: Heat needed to melt 1 kg solid without temperature change

options.label: B
options.text: Heat needed to raise temperature by 1°C

questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion = heat to melt 1 kg solid (no temp change).

questions.questionText: What is the direction of conventional current?
questions.explanation: Conventional current = + to − (opposite to electron flow).
questions.subtopic: Electric current electron flow direction conventional

questions.questionText: What does potential difference (voltage) measure?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy transferred per unit charge between two points

options.label: B
options.text: Number of electrons in a wire

questions.explanation: Voltage = energy (J) per unit charge (C) between two points.
questions.subtopic: Potential difference voltage energy per charge

questions.questionText: What is electrical resistance?

options.label: A
options.text: Opposition to current flow in a conductor

questions.explanation: Resistance = opposition to current flow (measured in ohms).

questions.questionText: What does Ohm's law state?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law: V = I × R (voltage = current × resistance).
questions.subtopic: Ohm law V equals IR relationship

questions.questionText: In a series circuit with 3 bulbs, what happens when one bulb blows?
questions.explanation: Series: if one bulb breaks, circuit is broken → all bulbs off.
questions.subtopic: Series circuit current same each component

questions.questionText: In a household circuit, appliances are connected in:
questions.explanation: Household = parallel (each appliance independently gets full 240V).
questions.subtopic: Parallel circuit voltage same each branch

questions.questionText: A bulb uses 240 V and 0.5 A. What is its power?
questions.subtopic: Electric power P equals VI calculation

questions.questionText: What unit is used for household electricity consumption?
questions.explanation: Household electricity = kWh (energy used over time).

questions.questionText: How does a fuse protect a circuit?

options.label: A
options.text: Melts and breaks circuit when current is too high

questions.explanation: Fuse = thin wire that melts and breaks if current exceeds safe limit.
questions.subtopic: Fuse safety device melts high current

questions.questionText: What is the function of the earth wire in a 3-pin plug?

options.label: A
options.text: Carries leakage current safely to ground

questions.explanation: Earth wire = safety wire (prevents electric shock from faults).
questions.subtopic: Three pin plug live neutral earth safety

questions.questionText: What does DNA stand for?
questions.explanation: DNA = Deoxyribonucleic Acid (genetic material).

questions.questionText: Where is a gene located in a cell?

options.label: A
options.text: On a chromosome in the nucleus

questions.explanation: Gene = section of DNA located on a chromosome in the nucleus.
questions.subtopic: Gene basic unit inheritance section DNA

questions.questionText: What is a chromosome made of?
questions.explanation: Chromosome = long thread of DNA wrapped with protein (histones).

questions.questionText: What is an allele?

options.label: A
options.text: A different form of a gene

questions.explanation: Allele = variant form of a gene (e.g., B or b for eye colour).

questions.questionText: In a heterozygous individual (Bb), which allele is expressed?
questions.explanation: Dominant allele = expressed in heterozygous condition (Bb shows B phenotype).

questions.questionText: A recessive trait is expressed in phenotype only when:
questions.explanation: Recessive trait shows only when genotype is homozygous recessive (bb).

questions.questionText: What is the genotype of an organism?
questions.explanation: Genotype = letters representing alleles (e.g., BB, Bb, bb).

questions.questionText: What is the phenotype of an organism?
questions.explanation: Phenotype = observable traits (e.g., tall, short, brown eyes).

questions.questionText: In a Punnett square for a cross between Bb × Bb, what fraction of offspring are heterozygous Bb?
questions.explanation: Bb × Bb → 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb → 50% (2/4) Bb heterozygous.

questions.questionText: What was Mendel's main contribution to genetics?

options.label: A
options.text: Laws of inheritance discovered through pea plant experiments

questions.explanation: Mendel established laws of inheritance (segregation, independent assortment).

questions.questionText: Which is the best way to write a scientific hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.text: If I change X, then Y will happen

questions.explanation: Hypothesis = 'If [variable], then [outcome]' (testable).

questions.questionText: The dependent variable is what the scientist:
questions.explanation: Dependent variable = measured outcome (responds to independent variable).

questions.questionText: What is one advantage of a bar chart over a data table?
questions.explanation: Bar charts allow quick visual comparison of categories.

questions.questionText: When is a pie chart most useful for displaying data?
questions.explanation: Pie chart = best for showing parts of a whole (percentages).

questions.questionText: Which type of graph is best for showing temperature change during a day?
questions.explanation: Line graph = continuous data over time (trends).
questions.subtopic: Line graph advantage trend over time

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of including a control group in an experiment?

options.label: A
options.text: To provide a baseline for comparison

questions.explanation: Control group = baseline (no treatment) to compare against experimental.

questions.questionText: Why is anecdotal evidence considered less scientifically reliable?

options.label: A
options.text: It is based on personal stories, not systematic study

questions.explanation: Anecdotal = personal accounts, not measurable/systematic.

questions.questionText: Why is a larger sample size preferred in scientific studies?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduces random error and improves reliability

questions.explanation: Larger sample = more representative + reduces random error.

questions.questionText: Which of these is an example of quantitative data?
questions.explanation: Quantitative = numerical (30°C). Qualitative = descriptive.

questions.questionText: Why do scientists replicate (repeat) each other's experiments?
questions.explanation: Replication = verifies results and ensures reproducibility.

questions.questionText: What property of the cell membrane allows it to control what enters and leaves the cell?
questions.explanation: Selective permeability = membrane controls what passes through.
questions.subtopic: Animal cell membrane selective permeability property

questions.questionText: What are plastids in plant cells?
questions.explanation: Plastids = family of organelles (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts).

questions.questionText: Osmosis involves the movement of which substance across a semi-permeable membrane?
questions.explanation: Osmosis = water movement across semi-permeable membrane.

questions.questionText: In diffusion, particles move from:

options.label: A
options.text: High concentration to low concentration (down gradient)

questions.explanation: Diffusion = particles move down concentration gradient (high → low).
questions.subtopic: Diffusion net particle movement high low

questions.questionText: Active transport requires energy because particles move:
questions.explanation: Active transport = against gradient (requires ATP energy).

questions.questionText: In which stage of mitosis do chromosomes become visible?
questions.explanation: Prophase = chromosomes condense and become visible.

questions.questionText: What is the main result of meiosis?
questions.explanation: Meiosis = produces 4 haploid gametes (n) from one diploid (2n) cell.

questions.questionText: Why are stem cells important in medicine?

options.label: A
options.text: They can develop into many different cell types

questions.explanation: Stem cells = undifferentiated cells that can become specialised cells.

questions.questionText: What is the basic cause of cancer?

options.label: A
options.text: Uncontrolled cell division due to mutations

questions.explanation: Cancer = uncontrolled cell division (caused by gene mutations).

questions.questionText: What is a tissue?

options.label: A
options.text: A group of similar cells working together

questions.explanation: Tissue = group of similar cells performing same function.
questions.subtopic: Tissue similar cells working together structure

questions.questionText: Where is glycogen stored in the body?
questions.explanation: Glycogen = animal storage form of carbohydrate (liver + muscles).

questions.questionText: Why is high blood cholesterol a health concern?

options.label: A
options.text: It can clog arteries (heart disease risk)

questions.explanation: High cholesterol accumulates in arteries → heart disease risk.
questions.subtopic: Cholesterol fat lipid blood level concern

questions.questionText: Why are omega-3 fatty acids considered healthy?

options.label: A
options.text: They support heart and brain health

questions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids (found in fish) support heart and brain function.
questions.subtopic: Omega 3 fatty acid fish heart health

questions.questionText: What is the role of antioxidants like Vitamin C and E?
questions.explanation: Antioxidants = neutralise harmful free radicals, protecting cells.
questions.subtopic: Antioxidant vitamin C E free radicals

questions.questionText: What is a common symptom of food poisoning?
questions.explanation: Food poisoning = bacteria/virus in food → vomiting, diarrhoea.

questions.questionText: Why does refrigeration preserve food?
questions.explanation: Refrigeration = low temperature slows bacterial reproduction.

questions.questionText: What is pasteurisation?

options.label: A
options.text: Heating milk briefly to kill harmful bacteria

questions.explanation: Pasteurisation = brief high heat to kill pathogens in milk.

questions.questionText: What is a function of food preservatives?

options.label: A
options.text: Extend shelf life by slowing spoilage

questions.explanation: Preservatives = extend food shelf life by slowing microbial growth.
questions.subtopic: Food additive preservative shelf life extended

questions.questionText: How is BMI calculated?
questions.explanation: BMI = weight (kg) / height² (m²). >25 = overweight, >30 = obese.
questions.subtopic: Obesity BMI body mass index over weight

questions.questionText: What is diabetes?

options.label: A
options.text: High blood sugar due to insulin problem

questions.explanation: Diabetes = body cannot regulate blood glucose (insulin issue).
questions.subtopic: Diabetes blood sugar level high condition

questions.questionText: How does temperature generally affect solubility of solids in water?
questions.explanation: For most solids, solubility increases as temperature rises.
questions.subtopic: Solute solubility rate temperature solid general

questions.questionText: Why does gas solubility decrease with temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: Gas molecules gain energy and escape solution

questions.explanation: Gas molecules gain kinetic energy and escape from solution when heated.

questions.questionText: Why do particles in a suspension settle over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Particles are large enough for gravity to pull them down

questions.explanation: Suspension particles are large → gravity pulls them down (settle).

questions.questionText: What is a property of a colloid?

options.label: B
options.text: Particles are visible only under microscope

questions.explanation: Colloid particles scatter light (Tyndall effect = visible light beam).
questions.subtopic: Colloid mixture particles scatter light Tyndall

questions.questionText: What is one property of a true solution?
questions.explanation: Solution = transparent, homogeneous mixture (light passes through).
questions.subtopic: Solution transparent light pass homogeneous mixture

questions.questionText: Why is water such a good solvent for many substances?
questions.explanation: Water polarity allows it to dissolve many ionic and polar substances.

questions.questionText: What is meant by hydration in chemistry?
questions.explanation: Hydration = water molecules cluster around dissolved ions/compounds.

questions.questionText: What is decanting?

options.label: A
options.text: Pouring liquid off a settled solid

questions.explanation: Decanting = carefully pouring liquid to separate from settled solid.

questions.questionText: How does a centrifuge separate mixtures?

options.label: A
options.text: Spinning creates force that separates by density

questions.explanation: Centrifuge = spins fast → denser components go to bottom.

questions.questionText: What defines a pure substance in chemistry?
questions.explanation: Pure substance = fixed chemical composition, constant properties.
questions.subtopic: Pure substance fixed composition constant properties

questions.questionText: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that:
questions.explanation: Arrhenius acid = produces H+ ions in aqueous solution.
questions.subtopic: Arrhenius acid produces hydrogen ions water

questions.questionText: According to Brønsted-Lowry, an acid is a:
questions.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry acid = proton (H+) donor.
questions.subtopic: Bronsted Lowry acid proton donor definition

questions.questionText: According to Brønsted-Lowry, a base is a:
questions.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry base = proton (H+) acceptor.
questions.subtopic: Bronsted Lowry base proton acceptor definition

questions.questionText: Which ion is characteristic of alkalis?
questions.explanation: Alkali = releases OH- (hydroxide) ions in water.
questions.subtopic: Hydroxide ion OH minus alkali characteristic

questions.questionText: Which ion is characteristic of acids?
questions.explanation: Acid = releases H+ (hydrogen) ions in water.
questions.subtopic: Hydrogen ion H plus acid characteristic

questions.questionText: What is a pH meter used for?
questions.explanation: pH meter = accurate digital device for measuring H+ concentration.
questions.subtopic: pH meter digital device accurate measurement

questions.questionText: How does pH paper work?

options.label: A
options.text: Paper changes colour depending on pH of solution

questions.explanation: pH paper (universal indicator paper) = changes colour at different pH.
questions.subtopic: pH paper universal indicator strip colour change

questions.questionText: What is a buffer solution?

options.label: A
options.text: Solution that resists changes in pH

questions.explanation: Buffer = mixture of weak acid + salt (resists pH change).
questions.subtopic: Buffer solution resist pH change weak acid

questions.questionText: What determines if a salt is acidic, basic, or neutral?

options.label: A
options.text: The strength of the original acid and base

questions.explanation: Salt character depends on whether acid and base are strong/weak.
questions.subtopic: Salt types acidic basic neutral character

questions.questionText: What type of compound is formed by the reaction between an acid and alkali?
questions.explanation: Acid + alkali = salt (ionic compound) + water.
questions.subtopic: Ionic compound acid alkali reaction neutralisation

questions.questionText: Distance is a scalar quantity because it has only:
questions.explanation: Distance = scalar (magnitude only, no direction).
questions.subtopic: Distance total path length scalar quantity

questions.questionText: Displacement differs from distance because displacement is:

options.label: A
options.text: The straight line from start to end (vector)

questions.explanation: Displacement = straight line vector from start to end position.
questions.subtopic: Displacement straight line initial final position vector

questions.questionText: How is speed calculated?
questions.explanation: Speed = total distance / time.
questions.subtopic: Speed calculated total distance divided time

questions.questionText: How is velocity calculated?
questions.explanation: Velocity = displacement / time (vector quantity).

questions.questionText: Acceleration measures the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: Acceleration = rate of change of velocity (Δv/Δt).

questions.questionText: What is momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity (p = mv, vector).

questions.questionText: What is impulse?
questions.explanation: Impulse = F × t = change in momentum.

questions.questionText: Force is defined as:

options.label: A
options.text: A push or pull on an object

questions.explanation: Force = a push or pull that can change object's motion.
questions.subtopic: Force applied push pull measured newton

questions.questionText: What unit is the SI derived unit for force, abbreviated N?
questions.explanation: SI unit of force = newton, symbol N.
questions.subtopic: Newton unit force measurement symbol N

questions.questionText: What is a resultant force?

options.label: A
options.text: Net (vector sum) force acting on object

questions.explanation: Resultant force = vector sum of all forces on object.
questions.subtopic: Resultant force net vector sum forces

questions.questionText: Which describes an opaque material?
questions.explanation: Opaque = no light transmitted through (e.g., wood, metal).
questions.subtopic: Opaque material no light pass through

questions.questionText: Which describes a transparent material?
questions.explanation: Transparent = light passes through clearly (e.g., glass, water).

questions.questionText: Which describes a translucent material?
questions.explanation: Translucent = allows partial light + diffuses (e.g., frosted glass).

questions.questionText: What is a shadow?

options.label: A
options.text: Region blocked from light by an opaque object

options.label: B
options.text: Dark area in a room at night

questions.explanation: Shadow = area where light from source is blocked by opaque object.
questions.subtopic: Shadow region blocked from light source

questions.questionText: What is the umbra of a shadow?

options.label: A
options.text: The dark central region of a shadow

questions.explanation: Umbra = completely dark central part of shadow (no light reaches).
questions.subtopic: Umbra dark central part of shadow

questions.questionText: What is the penumbra of a shadow?
questions.explanation: Penumbra = partial shadow region (some light reaches from extended source).
questions.subtopic: Penumbra lighter outer part of shadow

questions.questionText: During a solar eclipse, what is the order of celestial bodies?
questions.explanation: Solar eclipse = Moon passes between Sun and Earth.
questions.subtopic: Solar eclipse moon between sun earth

questions.questionText: During a lunar eclipse, what is the order of celestial bodies?

options.label: A
options.text: Sun, Earth, Moon (Earth blocks sun light)

questions.explanation: Lunar eclipse = Earth is between Sun and Moon (Earth's shadow on Moon).
questions.subtopic: Lunar eclipse earth between sun moon

questions.questionText: What is dispersion of light?

options.label: A
options.text: Splitting of white light into colours (spectrum)

questions.explanation: Dispersion = white light splits into colours when passing through prism.
questions.subtopic: Dispersion white light split colours prism

questions.questionText: How is a rainbow formed?

options.label: A
options.text: Dispersion + reflection of light in raindrops

questions.explanation: Rainbow = sunlight dispersed by water droplets (dispersion + reflection).

questions.questionText: What does a thermometer measure?
questions.explanation: Thermometer = measures temperature (not heat directly).

questions.questionText: Which is the SI base unit of temperature?
questions.explanation: SI unit of temperature = kelvin (K, no degree symbol).

questions.questionText: On the Celsius scale, at what temperature does pure water boil at sea level?
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C (sea level, 1 atm pressure).

questions.questionText: What is heat capacity of a substance?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy required to raise substance temperature by 1°C

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum temperature a substance can reach

questions.explanation: Heat capacity = energy (J) to raise temperature by 1°C.
questions.subtopic: Heat capacity energy raise temperature substance

questions.questionText: What is the melting point of a substance?

options.label: A
options.text: Temperature at which solid becomes liquid

questions.explanation: Melting point = temperature where solid changes to liquid.
questions.subtopic: Melting point temperature solid becomes liquid

questions.questionText: What is the boiling point of a substance?

options.label: A
options.text: Temperature at which liquid becomes gas (throughout)

questions.explanation: Boiling point = temperature where liquid changes to gas (boiling throughout).
questions.subtopic: Boiling point temperature liquid becomes gas

questions.questionText: What happens during condensation?

options.label: A
options.text: Gas changes to liquid and releases heat

questions.explanation: Condensation = gas → liquid (releases latent heat to surroundings).
questions.subtopic: Condensation gas becomes liquid release heat

questions.questionText: What is evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid at surface changes to gas below boiling point

questions.explanation: Evaporation = liquid → gas at surface (below boiling point).

questions.questionText: What happens during freezing?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid changes to solid and releases heat

questions.explanation: Freezing = liquid → solid (releases heat to surroundings).
questions.subtopic: Freezing liquid becomes solid release heat

questions.questionText: What is sublimation?

options.label: A
options.text: Solid changes directly to gas (without liquid phase)

questions.explanation: Sublimation = solid → gas directly (e.g., dry ice, naphthalene).
questions.subtopic: Sublimation solid directly gas without liquid

questions.questionText: What is an electric circuit?

options.label: A
options.text: A closed loop path for electric current

questions.explanation: Electric circuit = closed loop allowing current to flow continuously.
questions.subtopic: Electric circuit closed loop path current flow

questions.questionText: What does a battery provide in a circuit?

options.label: A
options.text: Electrical energy from chemical reactions (DC source)

questions.explanation: Battery = converts chemical energy → electrical energy (DC source).
questions.subtopic: Battery cell DC source chemical energy electrical

questions.questionText: What happens when a switch is open?
questions.explanation: Open switch = breaks circuit → no current flow.
questions.subtopic: Switch open break circuit stop current

questions.questionText: What happens when a switch is closed?
questions.explanation: Closed switch = completes circuit → current flows normally.
